FINRA and AI in 2026: What Broker-Dealers Must Record and Supervise

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

FINRA has no AI-specific rule; it applies its technology-neutral rules, so broker-dealers must supervise AI use under Rule 3110 and keep AI-related books and records under Rule 4511 and SEA Rule 17a-4. Its 2026 oversight report adds that firms using agents should consider how to track agent actions and decisions.

Broker-dealers ask the same question about every AI tool: what does FINRA expect us to keep, and who must check it? The answer comes from rules written long before generative AI, read through FINRA's recent reports and notices. Our pillar guide Regulators want the chain, not the model compares FINRA with US bank, UK and EU expectations.

This page summarises FINRA and SEC texts and one law-firm summary, each labelled. It is not legal advice.

What does FINRA say about AI in 2026?

FINRA says its rules "continue to apply when firms use GenAI or similar technologies." The 2026 oversight report's generative AI section, released on 9 December 2025 according to Debevoise & Plimpton, is the main statement of what examiners will look at.

The report defines AI agents as "systems or programs that are capable of autonomously performing and completing tasks on behalf of a user." It lists seven risks: autonomy, scope and authority, auditability and transparency, data sensitivity, domain knowledge, rewards and reinforcement, and the general risks of generative AI such as bias, hallucination and privacy. On auditability it warns that "complicated, multi-step agent reasoning tasks can make outcomes difficult to trace or explain."

The report then lists considerations for firms using agents:

  • "how to monitor agent system access and data handling;"
  • where to place human-in-the-loop oversight;
  • "how to track agent actions and decisions;" and
  • how to set guardrails "to limit or restrict agent behaviors, actions or decisions."

These are considerations, not rule text. They show what an examiner is likely to ask.

Which FINRA and SEC rules apply to AI tools?

Supervision, communications and books-and-records rules apply, because they are technology-neutral. Regulatory Notice 24-09 states that FINRA's rules apply to AI "just as they apply when member firms use any other technology or tool."

What must broker-dealers record when they use AI?

At a minimum, the records any rule already requires, plus the evidence that supervision worked. The 2026 report's generative AI practices go further, naming prompt and output logs and the model version used.

Three record types matter most:

  • Communications. An AI-drafted message sent to a customer is a communication like any other. SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4) covers originals received and copies sent that relate to the firm's "business as such."
  • Supervisory evidence. Rule 3110 requires a supervisory system. For AI, the evidence is who reviewed an output, what they saw and what they did. Notice 26-14 would add a duty to keep evidence that supervisory procedures were implemented and provide it on request.
  • Agent activity. The report's question on tracking agent actions and decisions implies a log of each tool call and decision, joined to the request and the approval.

Some questions remain open. In Regulatory Notice 25-07 of 14 April 2025, FINRA asked "what are members' recordkeeping challenges regarding AI-generated communications", naming chatbot communications and transcripts. It noted that "business as such" is not defined in the rule. Our AI audit trail checklist sets out the fields that cover all three record types.

How long must AI records be kept?

Usually three or six years, depending on the record type. Rule 4511(b) sets "at least six years" for FINRA records with no specified period. SEA Rule 17a-4(a) sets six years for core records, the first two in an easily accessible place. Rule 17a-4(b) sets three years for communications.

Format matters as much as duration. Under Rule 17a-4(f)(2), an electronic recordkeeping system must either keep a complete, time-stamped audit trail of modifications and deletions, with the identity of the person acting, or keep records "exclusively in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format." It must also be able to download records and their audit trails in human-readable and usable electronic formats. A prompt log in an editable application table meets neither test.

How should firms supervise AI agents?

By deciding in advance where a person approves, what the agent may touch, and how its actions are logged. The 2026 report's considerations map onto three controls: access and data-handling monitoring, human-in-the-loop review at defined points, and guardrails that restrict agent actions.

Debevoise & Plimpton's 12 December 2025 summary adds practical steps drawn from the report: formal review and approval processes combining business and technology expertise, documenting generative AI tools across their lifecycle, structured pre-deployment testing and ongoing monitoring. lowob's rule that nothing sends without a person is one way to set the review point; our explainer What is an approval gate? shows where the reviewer's action is captured.

What is changing in FINRA's rules?

Two proposals bear on AI. Regulatory Notice 26-14, published on 9 July 2026 with comments due by 11 September 2026, proposes replacing Rule 2210's principal pre-use approval of retail communications with risk-based supervisory standards. FINRA says that "applying the principal pre-use approval requirement to AI-generated retail communications can be challenging", and that generative AI tools may form part of a supervisory system "provided they are vetted, tested and monitored."

The notice also states that "members are responsible for their communications, regardless of whether they are generated by a human or AI technology." Notice 25-07, the 2025 request for comment on modernising workplace rules, asked about recordkeeping for AI-generated communications. Neither has produced a final rule change that we could find by mid-November 2026.

lowob takeaways

  • No AI rule, all the old ones. Supervision, communications and books-and-records rules apply to AI as to any tool.
  • Track agent actions. FINRA's 2026 report names auditability as an agent risk and asks how firms track actions and decisions.
  • Keep prompts, outputs and versions. The report suggests prompt and output logs and a record of which model version was used.
  • Store them properly. SEA Rule 17a-4(f) requires an audit-trailed or non-rewriteable system for electronic records.

Common questions

Does FINRA have rules specifically for AI?

No. FINRA states that its rules are intended to be technologically neutral and continue to apply when firms use generative AI. Supervision under Rule 3110, communications under Rule 2210 and books and records under Rule 4511 all apply. Its 2026 oversight report and Regulatory Notice 24-09 explain how examiners read those rules for AI tools and agents.

What does FINRA's 2026 report say about AI agents?

The 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report, released on 9 December 2025, defines AI agents as systems that autonomously perform tasks for a user. It lists seven risks, including autonomy, acting beyond authority and difficulty tracing multi-step reasoning, and asks firms to consider how they monitor agent access, place human oversight, track agent actions and decisions, and restrict agent behaviour.

Do AI-generated communications need to be retained by broker-dealers?

Yes, where they relate to the firm's business. SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4) requires originals of communications received and copies of communications sent relating to the firm's business as such to be kept for at least three years. FINRA states that firms are responsible for communications whether a human or AI technology generated them.

How long must broker-dealers keep AI logs?

It depends on what the log is. Records required by FINRA rules with no specified period are kept for at least six years under Rule 4511. Core records under SEA Rule 17a-4(a) are kept six years and communications three years. Electronic records must sit in an audit-trailed or non-rewriteable system under Rule 17a-4(f).
